These problems are compiled from Anaelise Sabbag's materials and *Sampling* by Sharon L. Lohr.


1. A well-designed survey measured attitudes of adult Americans toward college. A polling firm mailed this survey to 4,200 people across the United States and received 1,188 responses. No information was provided regarding the sampling frame used. Approximately 55% of those polled said they had major concerns about being able to pay for their child’s college education. Would you regard this figure as highly reliable and representative of the true proportion of adult Americans with this concern?  Tip: you can make assumptions about the sampling frame and discuss it as long as they are realistic assumptions.



2. For the following scenarios, identify possible sources of error and explain. Your explanation should note what KIND of sample was done and what the target population versus sampled population are. 

> Two well-designed customer satisfaction surveys were conducted in a large regional hospital in Florida in 2019. One survey was conducted by a paper survey sent by mail and the other by telephone interviews. To keep costs low, the telephone sample was interviewed by nursing staff on the evening shift, many of whom had cared for the former patients they were asked to call. All patients in that hospital in Florida in 2019 received one of those two-forms of the survey. The paper questionnaires showed much lower satisfaction ratings.

> Every year since 1927, Time magazine has chosen a Person of the Year to recognize a person or group who has had the most influence on the world that year. Although the final choice is made by the magazine's editors, readers can vote for a Person of the Year on the poll website. In 2018, the editors chose The Guardians—journalists who were murdered in 2018 for “speaking up and speaking out”—as the Person of the Year. The winner of the readers' poll was BTS, a K-pop band with a large online following.

> A survey is conducted to find the average weight of cows in a region. A list of all farms is available for the region, and 50 farms are selected at random. Then the weight of each cow at the 50 selected farms is recorded.

> A survey is conducted to find the average weight of cows in a region. A list of all farms is available for the region, and 50 farms are selected at random. Then the weight of each cow at the 50 selected farms is recorded.

3. University X administered a required survey to a sample of its students with the intent to estimate the proportion of University X students enrolled in a course during Spring 2025 who were first-generation students. Note: you can assume a random sample was taken from the sampling frame.
    a. What do you suggest as sampling units and sampling frame if we assume that the sampling unit is the same as observational unit? Be specific and realistic.
    b. Based on your answer to the previous question, discuss all possible nonobservation errors.
    c. What do you suggest as sampling units, observational units, and sampling frame if we assume that the sampling unit is different than the observational unit?


4. Each of the 10,000 shelves in a certain library is 300 cm long. To estimate how many books in the library need rebinding, a librarian takes a sample of 50 books using the following procedure: He first generates a random integer between 1 and 10,000 to select a shelf, and then generates a random number between 0 and 300 to select a location on that shelf. Thus, the pair of random numbers (2531, 25.4) would tell the librarian to include the book that is above the location 25.4 cm from the left end of shelf number 2531 in the sample. Does this procedure generate an SRS of the books in the library? Explain why or why not.



5. An SRS of size 30 is taken from a population of size 100. The sample values are given below:

```{r}
y <- c(8, 5, 2, 6, 6, 3, 8, 6, 10, 7, 15, 9,
       15, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 14, 3, 4, 17, 10, 
       6, 14, 12, 7, 8, 12, 9)
```

a. What is the sampling weight for each unit in the sample?
b. Use the sampling weights to estimate the population total $\tau$.
c. Is this equivalent to another estimator that we use? Why?


6. Discuss whether an SRS would be a good design choice for the following situations. What other designs might be used? If we haven't learned the name of the design, just describe what you think we should do. 
    a. For an e-mail survey of students, a sampling frame is available that contains a list of e-mail addresses for all students.
    b. A researcher wants to take a sample of patients of board-certified allergists.
    c. A researcher wants to estimate the percentage of topics in a medical website that have errors.
    d. A county election official wants to assess the accuracy of the machine that counts the ballots by taking a sample of the paper ballots and comparing the estimated vote tallies for candidates from the sample to the machine counts.

7. Cullen (1994) took a sample of the 580 children served by an Auckland family practice to estimate the percentage of children overdue for a vaccination.
    a. What sample size in an SRS would be necessary to estimate the proportion with a bound on the error of estimation of  0.1 (i.e. 1 percentage points)?
    b. Cullen actually took an SRS of size 120, of whom 93 were overdue for vaccination. Give a 95% CI for the proportion of children served by the practice who were overdue for vaccination.



8. What stratification variable(s) would you use for each of the following situations:
    a. A political poll to estimate the percentage of registered voters in Arizona who approve of the governor's performance.
    b. An e-mail survey of students at your university, to estimate the total amount of money students spend on textbooks in a term.
    c. A sample of high schools in New York City to estimate the number of schools that offer one or more classes in computer programming.
    d. A sample of public libraries in California to study the availability and usage of computer resources.
    e. A survey of anglers visiting a freshwater lake, to learn about which species of fish are preferred.
    f. An aerial survey to estimate the number of walrus in the pack ice near Alaska between 173∘ East and 154∘ West longitude.
    g. A survey of businesses to learn about policies for paid leave.



9. A forester wants to estimate the total number of farm acres planted with trees for a state. All the farms in the state are categorized according to size. There are a total of 86 farms of size I (0-200 acres); 72 farms of size II (200-400 acres); 52 farms of size III (400-600 acres), and 30 farms of size IV (600+ acres). Because the number of acres of trees varies considerably with the size of the farm, he decides to take random samples from each size. A stratified random sample of 40 farms was selected using proportional allocation. The data collection yields the results shown in the table below on number of acres planted in trees. The data can be downloaded here [10-farms.csv](10-farms.csv) and on Canvas.

      b. Use R to make side-by-side boxplots of the number of farm acres with trees by size of farm. 
      c. Based on (b) and (a), do you think the strata were set up effectively?
      d. Estimate the parameter of interest and the variance of your estimate. 
      e. Estimate the average number of tree acres in farms of size II along with the variance of the estimate.
      f. Assume the study is going to be performed yearly with a bound on the error of estimation of 5,000 acres. Find the overall sample size and allocation assumign this bound and using proportional allocation.
      g. Imagine this same study was conducted using the simple random sampling method. Suppose that the same observational units were selected. Which method (stratified random sampling or simple random sampling) is the best method to estimate the parameter of interest?

10. Investigators selected an stratified sample of 200 high school seniors from a population of 2000 for a survey of television-viewing habits, with an overall response rate of 75%. They stratified by GPA and had the following results:

| GPA	| 	$N_g$ |  $n_g$ | \# resp. $n^*_g$ | mean hours of television $\bar{y}_g$| $s_g$
|----|---|---|---|-----|---|
| 3.0 - 4.0 |	700|	75 | 66| 32 |	15 | 
| 2.0 - 2.99 |	800| 72| 58| 41	|19| 
| Below 2.0 |	500	| 53 |  26| 54	 | 25 | 

  a. What is the estimate for the average number of hours of television watched per week if only the respondents are analyzed? (Hint: pay attention to the fact that averages are given here!)
  b. Does is appear that the three GPA groups have the same or different response rates?
  c. Now estimate the mean hours of television watched per week taking the nonresponse into account.  (Hint: pay attention to the fact that averages are given here!)
  d. Was it important to adjust for nonresponse here? In which way did we expect our estimate to be biased (if at all) without adjusting for nonresponse?
